archetype.name: Retooling (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff has turned a bottom-ranked offense into a productive Kirk Cousins passing attack, but the defense and run game are too broken to support a winning team yet.

report.headline: Cousins fixed the offense; a last-ranked scoring defense keeps Las Vegas below .500.
report.take:
This is a very different Raiders team from the one that went 3-14 a year ago with the league's worst offense. Under first-year coach Klint Kubiak, with Cousins starting every week, Las Vegas scores 26.4 points a game (8th), up from 14.2 (32nd) in 2025. The engine is the passing game. Pass EPA sits 10th, the line has allowed only 11 sacks (2nd-best sack rate), and the targets run through tight ends and backs: Brock Bowers has 69 in seven games, Ashton Jeanty 55, Michael Mayer 46. It is a timing-and-middle-of-the-field offense, and it works.

The defense undoes it. The Raiders allow 29.8 points a game, the most in the league, with a success rate allowed that ranks 31st, a red-zone touchdown rate allowed of 71.1% (28th) and a third-down rate allowed that ranks 26th. The odd part is that the pass rush is real: the 3rd-best pressure rate and 14 takeaways (4th). This unit gets home sometimes and grabs the ball, but on the snaps when it doesn't, offenses move at will underneath (short-pass EPA allowed ranks 32nd) and on the ground (explosive run rate allowed 31st). Kansas City, the Rams and San Francisco each ran for close to 200 yards.

The schedule split hides how fragile this is. The Raiders opened with wins over Miami, the Chargers and New Orleans, whose offenses now rank 26th, 32nd and 22nd. Since then they have lost most of their games, and every loss came to an offense ranked 11th or better. Their only win in that stretch was a 38-33 shootout with the Jets. The 4-5 record is slightly flattering: a -30 point differential implies 3.4 wins, and covering two-thirds of their spreads says the market keeps underrating the offense rather than that the team is good.

The run game is the other structural problem, and it is not about game script. At 3.01 yards a carry, 1.39 yards before contact and a 31st-ranked stuff rate, the line simply isn't creating anything for Jeanty. Yet the Raiders still run slightly more than expected (pass rate over expected -2.1). Until that changes, the offense lives on Cousins' arm, and a defense that shuts down the short game can choke it out.

strengths.title: Cousins-led efficient passing game
strengths.body: Pass EPA ranks 10th and the offense scores at an 8th-ranked clip despite a run game near the bottom of the league. Cousins has thrown for 300-plus yards in four games, and the volume to Bowers, Jeanty and Mayer keeps the ball moving underneath. It is a real, sustainable shift from 2025 and the clearest sign the new staff's scheme fits him.

strengths.title: Pass protection keeps Cousins clean
strengths.body: Only 11 sacks allowed, the 2nd-best sack rate, and line penalties ranked 2nd-fewest. The pressure rate allowed is only 21st, so part of this is Cousins getting the ball out and avoiding the worst outcomes. The same line that can't run block has protected him well enough, and that should hold.

strengths.title: Pass rush creates takeaways
strengths.body: A 3rd-ranked pressure rate and 14 takeaways (4th) are the defense's only real weapons, and they were behind the early wins: five sacks against Miami, four takeaways at New Orleans. The pressure is likely to keep coming. The takeaway pace leans on luck and should cool.

concerns.title: Defense bleeds on every non-pressure snap
concerns.body: Success rate allowed ranks 31st, short-pass EPA allowed is dead last, and red-zone touchdown rate allowed is 28th. That is why a top-3 pass rush coexists with the most points allowed in the league. This is a structural flaw, not bad luck, and it has gotten worse against competent offenses.

concerns.title: Run game that can't move
concerns.body: At 3.01 yards a carry (32nd), 1.39 yards before contact (32nd) and a run EPA of -0.234, the problem starts at the line, not with Jeanty. Even so, the offense runs slightly more than expected, wasting downs and putting Cousins in long-yardage spots. Without a fix up front, this won't improve.

concerns.title: Gashed by explosive runs
concerns.body: The defense allows the 31st-ranked explosive run rate. The Rams ran for 199 yards and San Francisco for 190. Combined with a 30th-ranked time of possession, opponents control games once they get going.

trend.note: The good start came against three weak offenses. Since then the Raiders have lost to every good offense they've faced, bottoming out with a five-turnover, 38-17 loss at San Francisco.

nextGame.headline: Raiders' pass rush meets a Seattle line missing two starters.
nextGame.body:
Seattle is close to the Raiders' mirror image: a 5th-ranked defense by EPA with the stingiest explosive-pass and deep-pass numbers in the league, paired with an offense ranked 23rd that runs often (pass rate over expected -5.9) and runs badly (rush EPA 28th). Its point differential says it is better than 5-4, and the Book makes it a 3.5-point favorite indoors in Las Vegas. Cousins' downfield shots should be scarce. But Seattle is only 21st against short passes, which is exactly where Bowers and Jeanty work, and its red-zone defense is 29th.

Availability tilts toward the Raiders. Seattle is without guard Quenton Nelson and tackle Charles Cross, both near-every-snap starters, in front of a line that already allows the league's highest pressure rate. Sam Darnold is out, and Drew Lock is questionable with an oblique strain, though he is expected to play through it. Defensive tackle Leonard Williams, linebacker Uchenna Nwosu and receiver Rashid Shaheed are also out. For Las Vegas, rotational DT Thomas Booker IV is out and backup center Trey Zuhn III is questionable after a concussion. Neither is a core piece.

waysToWin.title: Overwhelm Seattle's patched-up protection
waysToWin.body: The Raiders' 3rd-ranked pressure rate meets a line that allows the most pressure in the league, now missing Nelson and Cross, protecting a quarterback nursing an oblique. Seattle is also 26th in turnover differential. If the rush produces sacks and short fields, the Raiders' defense finally gets to play from ahead.

waysToWin.title: Live underneath with Bowers and Jeanty
waysToWin.body: Seattle shuts down deep throws but ranks 21st against short passes, and that is the core of this offense. Long drives of quick throws to the tight ends and backs can turn into touchdowns against a red-zone defense that ranks 29th. Winning the red zone is the most realistic way for the Raiders to outscore an elite defense.

waysToLose.title: Offense stalls against an elite defense
waysToLose.body: Seattle ranks 2nd in success rate allowed and 1st against deep passes. The Raiders' run game offers no relief at -0.234 EPA a carry. If the underneath game gets bottled up, the offense has no second option, and drives die on third-and-long.

waysToLose.title: Seattle's run game finds the soft spot
waysToLose.body: Seattle wants to run, and the Raiders allow the 31st-ranked explosive run rate and convert few third-down stops. Even a weak ground game could pile up long, clock-eating drives that shorten the night for Cousins.

waysToLose.title: Another turnover spiral
waysToLose.body: The Raiders gave the ball away five times in San Francisco. Against a defense this good, the offense can't spot Seattle short fields. A repeat would hand the game away regardless of the pass-rush matchup.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Raiders' edge rushers can turn Seattle's backup blockers and a sore Drew Lock into early sacks and takeaways. That is the one matchup where they hold a clear edge.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing offense is real and should keep the Raiders competitive, but the remaining schedule is lopsided. Denver twice, Kansas City, and a Cleveland defense ranked 11th will test the offense far more than September did. The Chargers, Tennessee and an Arizona defense ranked 29th are the clear chances to win. Expect scoring to drift down from the current pace against better defenses, and the takeaway rate to cool, which removes the defense's one source of help. The run defense and red-zone defense are structural problems that probably won't be fixed midseason.

The realistic path is a split of the soft games and the toss-ups, finishing a few games under or around .500, third in a division where Denver and Kansas City have pulled away. That is still a meaningful step up from 3-14 for a first-year staff. Wild-card hopes rest on stealing at least one game against Denver or Kansas City.
swingFactors: Whether the defense can tighten in the red zone and on early downs
Turnover luck holding up on both sides

confidence.note: Nine games with one QB and a clear pattern by opponent quality, but takeaway luck and a back-loaded schedule add variance.
